Write-up text before the decision: on random $e_{3}$s Loss on correct $e_{3}$s Figure 7: In the semi-synthetic fact setup, models are capable of latent two-hop reasoning, achieving non-zero accuracy and a significant reduction in loss over a random baseline. We fine-tune Llama 3 8B Instruct models on 17 different synthetic “first-hop” fact datasets, connecting fictional people with real-world entities (e.g. “Nadia Hassan-Virtanen’s favorite programming language is Scala”) and rely on the model’s knowledge of the natural “second-hop” facts – attributes of these real-world entities (e.g. “The creator of Scala is Martin Odersky”). The results are averaged across models, each trained with three seeds on one of synthetic datasets consisting of around 20 ‘first-hop’ facts, and evaluated on questions about two to four attributes per dataset. A more detailed breakdown of the results is included in Appendix F. #### Results We find definitive evidence that LLMs are capable of latent two-hop reasoning. Across the 17 training dataset types (evaluated on 63 different question signatures total) we obtain (i) near–perfect accuracy on the newly taught first-hop questions ($>\!99\%$), (ii) high accuracy on the natural second-hop questions (average $\approx\!65\%$) and, most importantly, (iii) clear above-chance performance on two-hop questions without chain-of-thought. The average no-CoT accuracy rises to roughly 20% (Figure 7, left), compared with the near-zero performance observed in the fully–synthetic set-up of Section 2. Similarly, the no-CoT test loss drops well below the random-response baseline (Figure 7, right).
Previous context: In a semi-synthetic setup, a model is fine-tuned on 17 datasets linking fictional people to real-world entities and relies on its pretrained knowledge of attributes of those entities. Across 63 question types, it achieves over 99% first-hop accuracy, about 65% second-hop accuracy, and about 20% average two-hop accuracy without chain-of-thought, with loss well below a random baseline. Accuracy is far from perfect, and the setup mixes fine-tuned and pretrained knowledge.
Previous question: How far should the team accept this result as evidence that the model performs latent two-hop reasoning?

=== key 841f792dcc16
Kind of decision: how strongly to state a claim
Problem: How strongly to state conclusions about reasoning capabilities
Write-up text before the decision: u et al. (2024) train models to use meaningless filler tokens (e.g., ‘…’) instead of CoT to solve reasoning tasks; this setup can be seen as an intermediate between CoT and no-CoT. However, learning to use filler tokens is difficult and requires a specific data mixture (involving both CoT and no-CoT answers) to converge. A related line work work focused on distilling CoT reasoning, i.e. training models to zero-shot give answers similar to those they would give after CoT (Zelikman et al., 2022; 2024; Hsieh et al., 2023; Mukherjee et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2024). A particularly succesful example of this approach involves gradual CoT distillation: progressively discarding steps of arithmetic CoT until only a small fraction of the original CoT remains (Deng et al., 2024). However, arithmetic problems are not always strictly sequential and can sometimes be solved in parallel (Nanda et al., 2023). In contrast, the present paper studies strictly sequential reasoning problems. ## 8 Conclusion Our results highlight how experimental design fundamentally shapes conclusions about LLM reasoning capabilities. Models that completely fail at latent two-hop reasoning when learning synthetic facts separately (0% accuracy and no loss improvement over random chance) succeed when those same facts co-occur in training documents or when one fact comes from pretraining rather than fine-tuning. Conversely, frontier models’ apparent success on real-world two-hop questions may reflect memorization or facts co-occurring in training data rather than genuine compositional reasoning.
Previous context: A team has found that models fail completely at latent two-hop reasoning when two synthetic facts are learned separately, but succeed when the facts co-occur in training documents or when one fact comes from pretraining. They also note that frontier models' success on real-world two-hop questions could stem from memorization or co-occurrence in training data. They are writing the conclusion about what these results imply for LLM reasoning capabilities.

Write-up text before the decision: n answering questions. The benchmark focuses on detecting imitative falsehoods: errors that arise from training models on internet text, such as common misconceptions or fictional concepts. Each benchmark entry features a question with several correct and incorrect reference answers. Initially, TruthfulQA was intended for open-ended generation (not multiple-choice), evaluated through human labeling or automated evaluation. To support these evaluations, many reference answers were designed as paraphrases of other answers to ensure good coverage. We also introduced a multiple-choice version of TruthfulQA called MC1, where one correct answer is paired with 4-5 incorrect options. In the original paper and codebase, this metric was computed by taking the logprobs for each answer and selecting the highest. However, it has become common for people to test models by showing them all answer choices at once and asking them to pick one. This setup can admit simple test-taking heuristics, such as selecting the “odd-one-out” answer (as discussed in Alex Turner’s post). In particular, if multiple incorrect options are paraphrases of each other, then a model can do much better than chance by simply avoiding these paraphrased options. This may cause the multiple-choice format to measure a model’s test-taking ability rather than its truthfulness. Our evaluations in 2021/2 suggested that models were not significantly exploiting such heuristics, but it remains a possibility with new models and different post-training and prompting strategies. ## New binary-choice setting To address this,

Write-up text before the decision: New, improved multiple-choice TruthfulQA | Truthful AI # New, improved multiple-choice TruthfulQA - January 15, 2025 Owain Evans, James Chua, Stephanie Lin ## TLDR There is a potential issue with the multiple-choice versions of our TruthfulQA benchmark (a test of truthfulness in LLMs), which could lead to inflated model scores. This issue was analyzed by a helpful post by Alex Turner. We created a new multiple-choice version of TruthfulQA that fixes the issue. We compare models on the old and new versions and find very similar performance. This suggests that models are not exploiting the issue in the old versions to a significant extent, and so past results on the old versions are likely valid.

Write-up text before the decision: out” heuristics and to ensure more interpretable results. ## Correlation between general capabilities and scores on TruthfulQA When TruthfulQA was first released, large state-of-the-art models like GPT-3 showed inverse scaling, where they performed worse due to their improved ability to model the errors inherent in the pretraining data. However, as the plot above shows, highest-scoring models are now often the most generally capable ones (e.g. Claude 3.5 Sonnet). This raises the question of how well TruthfulQA measures safety vs. capabilities in current models (see this paper). First, we emphasized that TruthfulQA covers only a narrow aspect of truthfulness, which is itself only one part of model safety. Second, the correlation between capabilities and safety is partly explained by model post-training (e.g. RLHF) that targets truthfulness. TruthfulQA depends on background knowledge (capabilities) and a truthful orientation (safety). If (hypothetically) all labs achieved strong truthful orientation via post-training, then a large part of the remaining variance across models would be explained by capabilities. But this would not mean that TruthfulQA is unhelpful: TruthfulQA (or questions inspired by it) may be a target during the development of post-training. (Note: It seems that models do not generally have a perfect “truthful orientation” from post-training.) We also note that in recent models TruthfulQA performance seems to improve with scaling of base models (without post-training). That is, the inverse scaling trend does not continue even for base models. That said,

=== key 780acdafedee
Kind of decision: which experiment or hypothesis to pursue
Problem: Questions about past events could be answered by models simply memorizing outcomes, so forecasting ability could not be tested fairly.
Write-up text before the decision: pertise, forecasting is only used for a small number of questions. This motivates using ML to automate forecasting, e.g. by automating human information retrieval (finding news sources), reasoning (to decide if some evidence bears on a forecast), and quantitative modeling. ML models may also have some advantages over human forecasters. Models can read through text or data much faster than humans and can discern patterns in noisy high-dimensional data that elude humans. When it comes to learning, humans cannot be trained on past data (e.g. How likely was the Soviet Union’s collapse from the viewpoint of 1980?) because they know the outcomes -- but past data can be used to train ML models (“retrodiction”). As a step towards automating human forecasting, we introduce *Autocast*, a new dataset for measuring ML models' forecasting ability. Autocast includes thousands of forecasting questions collected from human forecasting tournaments ([Metaculus](https://www.metaculus.com/), [Good Judgment Open](https://www.gjopen.com/), [CSET Foretell](https://cset.georgetown.edu/publication/future-indices/)). The questions vary in the forecasting horizon from days to decades, in the topic (including politics, economics and science), and in the answer format (e.g. multiple-choice vs. predicting a number). The questions are pre-selected for public interest, and there is a strong human baseline (the crowd aggregate of many competitive forecasters). The questions in Autocast are about past events (e.g. the US 2020 election) and so ML models could answer them simply by memorizing what happened.
Previous context: A research team is building a dataset of thousands of forecasting questions drawn from human forecasting tournaments, to measure ML models' ability to forecast. The questions cover many topics, horizons and answer formats, and a strong human crowd baseline exists. The questions concern events that have already happened, so a model trained on recent text could answer them by recalling the outcomes instead of forecasting.
Previous question: How should the team set up the benchmark so that it tests forecasting (retrodiction) rather than memorization of outcomes?
